name: Yaur
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

earlier_scan.source_named: Kamholz, David. 2014. Austronesians in Papua (PhD diss., UC Berkeley) and Kamholz, Tone and language contact in southern Cenderawasih Bay — Yaur prosody discussed

new_statements.quote: Yaur has both contrastive tone and vowel length.[fn. 21: Yaur was not known to be tonal prior to my fieldwork.] There is rarely more than one long vowel in a word. The tone-bearing unit is the mora, with short vowels counted as a single mora, and long vowels and diphthongs counted as two moras. Two underlying tones are associated with moras: high (H) and low (L). It follows that contour tones can be realized only as the sequences HL and LH on long vowels and diphthongs. ... [p. 9 fn. 3:] Whether what I analyze as length or tone could be reanalyzed as stress (more plausible in some cases than others) has little impact on the complexity of the system and the care with which it must be examined.
new_statements.citation: Kamholz, David. 2017. Tone and language contact in southern Cenderawasih Bay. NUSA: Linguistic studies of languages in and around Indonesia 62: 7-39 (= Kamholz 2014, Austronesians in Papua, PhD diss. UC Berkeley, sec. 5.3.3 p. 114, near-verbatim).
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.3 'Yaur', p. 25 (PDF p. 19) with fn. 21; caveat sec. 2 p. 9 fn. 3 (PDF p. 3)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yaur is described as a lexical tone language (H vs L per mora) with contrastive vowel length; the only modern description gives no word-stress rule and does not posit stress, noting only that some length/tone facts might alternatively be analysed as stress. Unlike its sister Yerisiam and neighbour Moor, no reflex of Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress is identified for Yaur ('no robust generalizations', Table 17 p. 28; diss. p. 117).
new_statements.exceptions: Author flags the analysis as 'a work in progress' (p. 10): in Yaur suprasegmental contrasts are neutralised in many phonological contexts, production is variable, and speakers treat the contrasts as optional (p. 9). Common tone patterns: disyllables H-L 202, L-H 176, HL-H 42, LH-L 36; trisyllables H-H-L 167, L-L-H 119, etc. (Table 13 p. 26).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone on citation forms from a 1342-word lexicon; no phrase-level prosody described.
new_statements.identity_note: Kamholz's Yaur data are from his own 2010-2013 fieldwork (speakers from the Sima/Yaur coast, Nabire regency); the language-level glottocode yaur1239 applies directly, no dialect split is described. Yaur forms the Yaur-Yerisiam subgroup (yaur1240) with Yerisiam (ires1239), whose Kamholz./ires1239/ (hard-linked here).

sources.note: Same analysis as 2014 (tone + length, mora TBU, H/L). p. 9: in Moor and Yaur 'suprasegmental contrasts are neutralized in many phonological contexts and production is quite variable'; fn. 3: 'Whether what I analyze as length or tone could be reanalyzed as stress (more plausible in some cases than others) has little impact on the complexity of the system'. Table 17: 'Yaur: No robust generalizations' (no reflex of Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress identified). No word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Kamholz, David C. 2014. Austronesians in Papua: Diversification and change in South Halmahera-West New Guinea. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. (Yaur = ch. 5 sec. 5.3.3 p. 114, Tables 5.19-5.22 pp. 115-116; sec. 5.4 pp. 116-118)
sources.note: Yaur analysed as a tone language with contrastive vowel length (TBU = mora, underlying H and L); no synchronic word-stress statement. p. 117 lists SHWNG languages with penultimate stress or traces of it (Ma'ya, Moor, Yerisiam, Buli, Sawai, Taba, Ambai, Wandamen, Waropen, Warembori) -- Yaur is not among them.

sources.note: Headwords carry tone diacritics (acute H, grave L) and length (doubled vowels); no stress marks and no prose on prosody. (First page of entries saved.)
